extraction_notes.note: Mathpix PDF conversion: no environments, labels or numbered \section commands (sections 1-6 are inline '2. Preliminaries.' paragraphs), so every node is prose and every section field is empty.
Author 'Definition.' paragraphs that introduce several used terms in separate sentences were split one node per sentence, following the introduced-terms rule rather than the author's paragraph.
Proof of Theorem 5.2 is a sketch ('we can show that this contradicts Theorem 3.3') without a closing square; Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.3 marked semi_formal.

Cited facts stated in prose ('As has been noted before ... [FSS]', 'It is known that C_k is unbounded') typed theorem/external rather than remark; TP1 is the implicit link from Exactly-n to Threshold in Theorem 3.5 and Corollary 5.3.
The upper-bound cost log chi_k(n)+k is only announced in the section 4 introduction; kept as a main claim supported by the protocol AP1 and Theorem 4.1.

nodes.name: Poker players (number on forehead) example
nodes.statement: For example, suppose $k$ poker players are sitting around a table, and each one is holding a number to his forehead for the others to see. This situation fits our model and we can determine how many bits the players need to communicate in order for all of them to know if the sum of the numbers is greater than $n$.
nodes.statement_short: k players each see all numbers but their own and must decide whether the sum exceeds n.

nodes.name: MPP communication model (cyclic broadcast)
nodes.statement: For simplicity, we only allow the parties to communicate as follows. At time $t=0$, process $P_{0}$, examining the numbers it knows, broadcasts one bit. At time $t=1$, process $P_{1}$, examining the numbers it knows, and the bit sent by $P_{0}$, broadcasts one bit. This continues in a cyclic fashion until, at a prearranged time , the processes are required to halt, with either all accepting or all rejecting.
nodes.statement_short: Processes broadcast one bit each in cyclic order P_0, P_1, ..., until a prearranged halting time, then all accept or all reject.

nodes.name: Multi-party shared-information protocol (MPP)
nodes.statement: In this paper we prove both upper and lower bounds on the complexity of multi-party, shared-information protocols (MPP's) for determining certain basic predicates of sets of integers.

nodes.name: k processes and k variables in [1,n]
nodes.statement: From now on we assume that there are $k$-processes $P_{0}, \ldots, P_{k-1}$, and $k$ variables $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{k}$ that range over the integers from 1 to $n$.

nodes.name: Number-on-forehead access model
nodes.statement: Each process has access to the $a_{j}$, except that $P_{i}$ is denied access to $a_{i}$.
also_stated_at: Formally, each $P_{i}$ has access to every $a_{j}$ except for $a_{i}$.

nodes.name: Broadcast history
nodes.statement: Definition. A broadcast history $b \in(0+1)^{*}$ is a record of all the bits transmitted by the processes up to a certain point in time.
nodes.genus: record of all the bits transmitted by the processes up to a certain point in time

nodes.name: k-party protocol
nodes.statement: DEFINITION. A $k$-party protocol, or just a protocol when $k$ is known, is a deterministic algorithm that, for each process $P_{i}$, determines from the numbers $P_{i}$ knows and the broadcast history, what bit $P_{i}$ should transmit at times $i, i+k, \ldots$.
differentia: for each process $P_{i}$, determines from the numbers $P_{i}$ knows and the broadcast history, what bit $P_{i}$ should transmit at times $i, i+k, \ldots$

nodes.name: Hypercube of situations H_n
nodes.statement: Definition. Let $H_{n}=\{1, \ldots, n\}^{k}$ be a $k$-dimensional hypercube.

nodes.name: Situation
nodes.statement: Each point $\left\langle v_{0}, v_{1}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right\rangle \in H_{n_{n}}$ describes a situation, or assignment to the variables $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{k-1}$.

nodes.name: Complete broadcast history Phi(v)
nodes.statement: DEFINITION. Let $\Phi$ be a protocol for $k$ processes working with integers in the range 1 to $n$. For each $\bar{v} \in H_{n}, \Phi$ determines a string $\Phi(\bar{v}) \in(0+1)^{*}$ that is the complete broadcast history for the processes in situation $\bar{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: A protocol assigns each situation its complete broadcast history string.

nodes.name: Valid assignment of broadcast histories
nodes.statement: DEFINITION. Let $Q$ be a $0-1$ predicate of $k$ integers in the range 1 to $n$. An assignment $\Phi$ of broadcast histories to $H_{n}$ is valid for $Q$ if, for every $\bar{v}, \bar{w} \in H_{n}$ that differ in exactly one component, $$ \Phi(\bar{v}) \neq \Phi(\bar{w}) \text { whenever } Q(\bar{v}) \neq Q(\bar{w}) . $$
differentia: for every $\bar{v}, \bar{w} \in H_{n}$ that differ in exactly one component, $$ \Phi(\bar{v}) \neq \Phi(\bar{w}) \text { whenever } Q(\bar{v}) \neq Q(\bar{w}) . $$
nodes.statement_short: An assignment is valid for Q if neighbours (differing in one coordinate) with different Q-values get different histories.

nodes.name: Valid protocol
nodes.statement: Definition. A protocol $\Phi$ is valid for a predicate $Q$ if $\Phi$ determines a valid broadcast history for $Q$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.1 (validity characterizes correct protocols)
nodes.statement: LEMMA 2.1. A $k$-party protocol $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ can be used by processes $P_{0}, \ldots, P_{k-1}$ to determine a predicate $Q$ if and only if $\Phi$ is valid for $Q$.
conclusions: A $k$-party protocol $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ can be used by processes $P_{0}, \ldots, P_{k-1}$ to determine a predicate $Q$ if and only if $\Phi$ is valid for $Q$
equivalent_conditions: A $k$-party protocol $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ can be used by processes $P_{0}, \ldots, P_{k-1}$ to determine a predicate $Q$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: Proof. Suppose $\Phi$ is not valid for $Q$. Then there are two points $\bar{w}$ and $\bar{v}$ such that \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] $Q(\bar{w}) \neq Q(\bar{v})$, \item[(b)] $\bar{w}$ and $\bar{v}$ differ only in coordinate $i$, and \item[(c)] $\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bar{w})=\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bar{v})$. \end{itemize} Since process $P_{i}$ cannot see coordinate $i$ it must behave in exactly the same way in situations $\bar{w}$ and $\bar{v}$. Thus, $P_{i}$ must accept or reject incorrectly at one of $\bar{w}$ or $\bar{v}$. Therefore, $\Phi$ cannot be used by the parties to correctly determine $Q$. The other direction is straightforward. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Contrapositive: an invalid protocol has two neighbouring points with equal histories but different Q, which P_i cannot distinguish.

nodes.name: Assume invalid: two bad neighbours
nodes.statement: Suppose $\Phi$ is not valid for $Q$. Then there are two points $\bar{w}$ and $\bar{v}$ such that
nodes.statement_short: Non-validity gives two points w, v with:

nodes.name: (a) different Q
nodes.statement: [(a)] $Q(\bar{w}) \neq Q(\bar{v})$,
nodes.statement_short: Q differs at w and v.

nodes.name: (b) neighbours
nodes.statement: [(b)] $\bar{w}$ and $\bar{v}$ differ only in coordinate $i$, and
nodes.statement_short: w, v differ only in coordinate i.

nodes.name: (c) same history
nodes.statement: [(c)] $\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bar{w})=\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bar{v})$.
nodes.statement_short: w, v have the same history.

nodes.name: P_i cannot distinguish
nodes.statement: Since process $P_{i}$ cannot see coordinate $i$ it must behave in exactly the same way in situations $\bar{w}$ and $\bar{v}$. Thus, $P_{i}$ must accept or reject incorrectly at one of $\bar{w}$ or $\bar{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: P_i behaves identically at w and v, so errs at one.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, $\Phi$ cannot be used by the parties to correctly determine $Q$. The other direction is straightforward. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Conclude Phi cannot determine Q; converse is easy.

nodes.name: Cost of a protocol
nodes.statement: DEFINITION. The cost of a protocol $\Phi$ on $H_{n}$ is the maximum length of a complete broadcast history on situations in $H_{n}$, i.e., $$ \operatorname{cost}_{\Phi}(n)=\max _{\bar{v} \in H_{n}}|\Phi(\bar{v})| . $$
nodes.genus: maximum length of a complete broadcast history on situations in $H_{n}$

nodes.name: Complexity of a predicate
nodes.statement: Definition. The complexity of a predicate $Q$ is the minimum, over all valid protocols $\Phi$ for $Q$, of the cost of $\Phi$.
nodes.genus: minimum, over all valid protocols $\Phi$ for $Q$, of the cost of $\Phi$

nodes.name: Exactly-n predicate
nodes.statement: Definition. The predicate Exactly-n is true of $k$ integers $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{k-1}$ if and only if $a_{0}+\cdots+a_{k-1}=n$.

nodes.name: Exactly-equal lower bounds imply threshold lower bounds
nodes.statement: As has been noted before, lower bounds on exactly-equal-to predicates imply lower bounds on threshold predicates (" $\sum a_{i} \geq n$ ") [FSS].
conclusions: lower bounds on exactly-equal-to predicates imply lower bounds on threshold predicates (" $\sum a_{i} \geq n$ ")

nodes.name: Accepting hyperplane S_n
nodes.statement: Let $S_{n}=\left\{\bar{v} \in H_{n} \mid \sum \bar{v}=n\right\}$ be the hyperplane on which the processes must "accept", as shown in Figure 1.

nodes.name: Forbidden k-pattern
nodes.statement: Definition. A set of $k$ distinct points $\bar{v}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}_{k-1} \in$ $H_{n}$ is a forbidden $k$-pattern if there is a point $\bar{w} \in H_{n}$ such that, for each $i, \bar{w}$ differs from $\bar{v}_{i}$ only in coordinate $i$.
differentia: there is a point $\bar{w} \in H_{n}$ such that, for each $i, \bar{w}$ differs from $\bar{v}_{i}$ only in coordinate $i$

nodes.name: Forbidden 3-patterns are equilateral triangles
nodes.statement: (For the case $k=3$, forbidden $k$-patterns on the plane $S_{n}$ are just equilateral triangles.)

nodes.name: Lemma 3.1 (forbidden pattern forces the apex history)
nodes.statement: LEMMA 3.1. Let $\Phi$ be a protocol for processes $P_{0}$, $\ldots, P_{k-1}$. Let $H_{n}=\{1, \ldots, n\}^{k}$ be the hypercube of situations, and let $\bar{w}=\left\langle w_{0}, \ldots, w_{k-1}\right\rangle$ be any point in $H_{n}$. If $\bar{v}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}_{k-1}$ is a forbidden $k$-pattern for $\bar{w}$, and the complete broadcast histories at the $\bar{v}_{j}$ are identical, i.e., $$ \alpha=\Phi\left(\bar{v}_{0}\right)=\Phi\left(\bar{v}_{1}\right)=\cdots=\Phi\left(\bar{v}_{k-1}\right), $$ then $\Phi(\bar{w})=\alpha$.
assumptions: Let $\Phi$ be a protocol for processes $P_{0}$, $\ldots, P_{k-1}$.
let $\bar{w}=\left\langle w_{0}, \ldots, w_{k-1}\right\rangle$ be any point in $H_{n}$
the complete broadcast histories at the $\bar{v}_{j}$ are identical
conclusions: $\Phi(\bar{w})=\alpha$
nodes.statement_short: If all points of a forbidden pattern for w share history alpha, then w also gets history alpha.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: Proof. By induction on the length of the broadcast history we prove that, for all $i$, the $i^{\text {th }}$ bit broadcast at $\bar{w}$ is the same as the $i^{\text {th }}$ bit broadcast at $\bar{v}_{i(\bmod k)}$.\\ Base: If $|\alpha|=0$, then every process immediately halts on $\bar{w}$ since it immediately halts on $\bar{v}_{i}$. Induction: Suppose, for all histories of length $<t$, the inductive hypothesis is true. Consider the $t^{\text {th }}$ bit to be broadcast. By induction, $P_{t(\bmod k)}$ sees the same broadcast history at $\bar{w}$ and at $\bar{v}_{t(\bmod k)}$, and hence, $P_{t(\bmod k)}$ broadcasts the same bit at time $t$ at $\bar{w}$ as it broadcasts at time $t$ at $\bar{v}_{t(\bmod k)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on time t: P_{t mod k} sees the same history at w and at v_{t mod k}, so broadcasts the same bit.

nodes.name: Induction statement
nodes.statement: By induction on the length of the broadcast history we prove that, for all $i$, the $i^{\text {th }}$ bit broadcast at $\bar{w}$ is the same as the $i^{\text {th }}$ bit broadcast at $\bar{v}_{i(\bmod k)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction: bit i at w equals bit i at v_{i mod k}.

nodes.name: Base
nodes.statement: Base: If $|\alpha|=0$, then every process immediately halts on $\bar{w}$ since it immediately halts on $\bar{v}_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Base case: empty history.

nodes.name: Induction
nodes.statement: Induction: Suppose, for all histories of length $<t$, the inductive hypothesis is true. Consider the $t^{\text {th }}$ bit to be broadcast. By induction, $P_{t(\bmod k)}$ sees the same broadcast history at $\bar{w}$ and at $\bar{v}_{t(\bmod k)}$, and hence, $P_{t(\bmod k)}$ broadcasts the same bit at time $t$ at $\bar{w}$ as it broadcasts at time $t$ at $\bar{v}_{t(\bmod k)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: P_{t mod k} sees identical histories.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.1 holds for all protocols
nodes.statement: Note that this Lemma is true for all protocols, not just valid ones.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.2 (monochromatic forbidden pattern invalidates)
nodes.statement: LEMMA 3.2. A $k$-party protocol $\Phi$ is not valid for the predicate Exactly- $n$ if it assigns the same broadcast history to all the points of a forbidden $k$-pattern of $S_{n}$.
assumptions: it assigns the same broadcast history to all the points of a forbidden $k$-pattern of $S_{n}$
conclusions: A $k$-party protocol $\Phi$ is not valid for the predicate Exactly- $n$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: Proof. Suppose $\bar{v}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}_{k-1}$, is a forbidden $k$-pattern on $S_{n}$ for the point $\bar{w}$, such that $$ \alpha=\Phi\left(\bar{v}_{0}\right)=\Phi\left(\bar{v}_{1}\right)=\cdots=\Phi\left(\bar{v}_{k-1}\right) . $$ By geometry, $\bar{w}$ is not on $S_{n}$, and by Lemma 3.1, $\Phi(\bar{w})=\alpha$. Therefore, $\Phi$ is not valid for Exactly- $n$. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: The apex w of the pattern lies off S_n but by Lemma 3.1 shares the pattern's history, violating validity.

nodes.name: Monochromatic pattern
nodes.statement: Suppose $\bar{v}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}_{k-1}$, is a forbidden $k$-pattern on $S_{n}$ for the point $\bar{w}$, such that $$ \alpha=\Phi\left(\bar{v}_{0}\right)=\Phi\left(\bar{v}_{1}\right)=\cdots=\Phi\left(\bar{v}_{k-1}\right) . $$
nodes.statement_short: Take a forbidden pattern on S_n with common history alpha.

nodes.name: Apex off S_n with same history
nodes.statement: By geometry, $\bar{w}$ is not on $S_{n}$, and by Lemma 3.1, $\Phi(\bar{w})=\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: w is off S_n and by Lemma 3.1 has history alpha.

nodes.name: Conclude invalid
nodes.statement: Therefore, $\Phi$ is not valid for Exactly- $n$. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Hence Phi is not valid.

nodes.name: chi_k(n)
nodes.statement: DEFINITION. The integer $\chi_{k}(n)$ is the smallest number . of colors required to color the points of $S_{n}$ so that no forbidden $k$-pattern on $S_{n}$ is colored monochromatically.
nodes.statement_short: Minimum colours for S_n with no monochromatic forbidden k-pattern.

nodes.name: Theorem 3.3 (lower bound via colorings)
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.3. The complexity of any $k$-party protocol for Exactly-n is bounded below by the logarithm of the number of colors required to color $S_{n}$ so that no forbidden $k$-patterns are colored monochromatically.
conclusions: The complexity of any $k$-party protocol for Exactly-n is bounded below by the logarithm of the number of colors required to color $S_{n}$ so that no forbidden $k$-patterns are colored monochromatically
nodes.statement_short: Complexity of Exactly-n is at least log chi_k(n).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.3
nodes.statement: Proof. Consider a protocol $\Phi$ for Exactly- $n$. Let each distinct broadcast history $\Phi(\bar{v})$, for $\bar{v} \in H_{n}$, define a color. If some forbidden $k$-pattern on $S_{n}$ is colored monochromatically, then, by Lemma 3.2, $\Phi$ is not valid for Exactly- $n$. This is a contradiction. Therefore, there must be more than $\chi_{k}(n)$ distinct broadcast histories, and hence, in some situation, at least $\log \left(\chi_{k}(n)\right)$ bits must be communicated. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Histories define a colouring of S_n; by Lemma 3.2 it has no monochromatic forbidden pattern, so it uses at least chi_k(n) colours.

nodes.name: Histories as colours
nodes.statement: Consider a protocol $\Phi$ for Exactly- $n$. Let each distinct broadcast history $\Phi(\bar{v})$, for $\bar{v} \in H_{n}$, define a color.
nodes.statement_short: Colour each situation by its broadcast history.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: If some forbidden $k$-pattern on $S_{n}$ is colored monochromatically, then, by Lemma 3.2, $\Phi$ is not valid for Exactly- $n$. This is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: A monochromatic forbidden pattern would contradict validity by Lemma 3.2.

nodes.name: Count histories
nodes.statement: Therefore, there must be more than $\chi_{k}(n)$ distinct broadcast histories, and hence, in some situation, at least $\log \left(\chi_{k}(n)\right)$ bits must be communicated. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: So at least chi_k(n) histories, hence log chi_k(n) bits.

nodes.name: B_k(n)
nodes.statement: Definition. Let $$ B_{k}(n)=\left\{\left(v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right) \mid 1 \leq v_{i} \leq n\right\} . $$

nodes.name: Unit vectors e_i
nodes.statement: For $0 \leq i \leq k-1$, let $\bar{e}_{i}$ be the vector whose $j^{\text {th }}$ coordinate is $\delta_{i j}$.

nodes.name: Gallai's Theorem
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.4. (Gallai [G,GRS]) For every c and k, there exists $a \lambda$ and an $n$, such that every $c$-coloring of $B_{k}(n)$ contains $k$ distinct vectors $$ \bar{v}, \bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{k-1} $$ that are identically colored.
conclusions: there exists $a \lambda$ and an $n$, such that every $c$-coloring of $B_{k}(n)$ contains $k$ distinct vectors $$ \bar{v}, \bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{k-1} $$ that are identically colored
nodes.statement_short: Multidimensional van der Waerden: any c-colouring of a large grid has a monochromatic homothetic simplex v, v+lambda e_i.

nodes.name: Theorem 3.5 (Threshold has superconstant MPP complexity)
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.5. Threshold has multi-party protocol complexity greater than any constant.
conclusions: Threshold has multi-party protocol complexity greater than any constant

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.5
nodes.statement: Proof. By Theorem 3.3 it suffices to prove that for a fixed $k, \chi_{k}(n)$ is unbounded. To get a contradiction, assume that $\chi_{k}(n)$ is bounded by some constant $c$. Define the projection $p$ from $S_{n}$ to $B_{k-1}(n)$ by $$ p\left(x_{0}, \ldots, x_{k-1}\right)=\left(x_{0}, \ldots, x_{k-2}\right) . $$ Since $\chi_{k}(n) \leq c$, there is a $c$-coloring $C$ of $S_{n}$ in which no forbidden $k$-pattern is colored monochromatically. The mapping $p$ is one-to-one, so $C$ and $p$ induce, in a natural way, a $c$-coloring of the points in $p\left(S_{n}\right)$. Consider a smaller set, $B_{k-1}(n / 4 k)$. It is a subset of $p\left(S_{n}\right)$ and is thus also $c$-colored via $p$. For large enough $n$, Gallai's Theorem implies the existence of $k-1$ distinct vectors $$ \bar{v}, \bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{k-2}, $$ in $B_{k-1}(n / 4 k)$ that are colored identically.\\ Let $\bar{v}=\left(v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-2}\right)$, and let $$ \bar{w}=\left(v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-2}, n-s-\lambda\right), $$ where $s=v_{0}+v_{1}+\cdots+v_{k-2}$. Since $s>0$ and $\lambda>0$, the last coordinate of $\bar{w}$ is $\leq n$. Furthermore, $1 \leq n-s-\lambda$ since $s$ is at most $(k-1) n / 4 k$ and $\lambda$ is at most $n / 4 k$. Thus, $\bar{w}$ is a situation in $H_{n}$. We now have a contradiction since the points $$ p^{-1}(\bar{v}), \quad p^{-1}\left(\bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{0}\right), \quad \ldots, \quad p^{-1}\left(\bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{k-2}\right) $$ form a monochromatic forbidden $k$-pattern for $\bar{w}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Theorem 3.3 show chi_k(n) unbounded: project S_n to B_{k-1}(n), apply Gallai to get a monochromatic simplex, whose lift is a monochromatic forbidden pattern. The key step builds the apex w with last coordinate n-s-lambda.

nodes.name: Reduce to unbounded chi
nodes.statement: By Theorem 3.3 it suffices to prove that for a fixed $k, \chi_{k}(n)$ is unbounded.
nodes.statement_short: By Theorem 3.3, suffices to show chi_k(n) unbounded.

nodes.name: Assume bounded
nodes.statement: To get a contradiction, assume that $\chi_{k}(n)$ is bounded by some constant $c$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume chi_k(n) <= c.

nodes.name: Define projection p
nodes.statement: Define the projection $p$ from $S_{n}$ to $B_{k-1}(n)$ by $$ p\left(x_{0}, \ldots, x_{k-1}\right)=\left(x_{0}, \ldots, x_{k-2}\right) . $$
nodes.statement_short: Project S_n onto first k-1 coordinates.

nodes.name: Good colouring C
nodes.statement: Since $\chi_{k}(n) \leq c$, there is a $c$-coloring $C$ of $S_{n}$ in which no forbidden $k$-pattern is colored monochromatically.
nodes.statement_short: Take a c-colouring C of S_n with no monochromatic forbidden pattern.

nodes.name: Induced colouring
nodes.statement: The mapping $p$ is one-to-one, so $C$ and $p$ induce, in a natural way, a $c$-coloring of the points in $p\left(S_{n}\right)$. Consider a smaller set, $B_{k-1}(n / 4 k)$. It is a subset of $p\left(S_{n}\right)$ and is thus also $c$-colored via $p$.
nodes.statement_short: C induces a c-colouring of B_{k-1}(n/4k) inside p(S_n).

nodes.name: Apply Gallai
nodes.statement: For large enough $n$, Gallai's Theorem implies the existence of $k-1$ distinct vectors $$ \bar{v}, \bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{k-2}, $$ in $B_{k-1}(n / 4 k)$ that are colored identically.
nodes.statement_short: Gallai gives a monochromatic v, v+lambda e_i in B_{k-1}(n/4k).

nodes.name: Define apex w
nodes.statement: Let $\bar{v}=\left(v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-2}\right)$, and let $$ \bar{w}=\left(v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-2}, n-s-\lambda\right), $$ where $s=v_{0}+v_{1}+\cdots+v_{k-2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define apex w with last coordinate n-s-lambda.

nodes.name: w is a situation
nodes.statement: Since $s>0$ and $\lambda>0$, the last coordinate of $\bar{w}$ is $\leq n$. Furthermore, $1 \leq n-s-\lambda$ since $s$ is at most $(k-1) n / 4 k$ and $\lambda$ is at most $n / 4 k$. Thus, $\bar{w}$ is a situation in $H_{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the last coordinate of w to lie in [1,n].

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: We now have a contradiction since the points $$ p^{-1}(\bar{v}), \quad p^{-1}\left(\bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{0}\right), \quad \ldots, \quad p^{-1}\left(\bar{v}+\lambda \bar{e}_{k-2}\right) $$ form a monochromatic forbidden $k$-pattern for $\bar{w}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lifted points form a monochromatic forbidden pattern for w.

nodes.name: Upper bound: log chi_k(n)+k bit protocol
nodes.statement: That is, we exhibit a cost $\left[\log \left(\chi_{k}(n)\right)+k\right]$-bit $k$-party protocol that is valid for the predicate Exactly- $n$.
conclusions: we exhibit a cost $\left[\log \left(\chi_{k}(n)\right)+k\right]$-bit $k$-party protocol that is valid for the predicate Exactly- $n$
nodes.statement_short: There is a valid protocol for Exactly-n using log chi_k(n)+k bits, matching the lower bound up to an additive constant.

nodes.name: Coloring protocol for Exactly-n
nodes.statement: Color the hyperplane $S_{n}=\left\{\bar{v} \in H_{n} \mid \sum \bar{v}=n\right\}$ of $H_{n}$ with $\chi_{k}(n)$ colors such that no forbidden $k$-pattern is monochromatic. Let $\left\langle v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right\rangle$ be a situation in $H_{n}$. Let process $P_{i}$ know every number but $v_{i}$. Each process $P_{i}$ computes the point $$ \bar{w}_{i}=\left\langle v_{0}, \ldots, v_{i-1}, n-\left(\sum_{j \neq i} v_{j}\right), v_{i+1}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right\rangle \in S_{n} . $$ At time $t=0, P_{0}$ broadcasts bit 0 of the color at $\bar{w}_{0}$. At $t=1, P_{1}$ broadcasts bit 1 of the color at $\bar{w}_{1}$. This continues until $\log \left(\chi_{k}(n)\right)$ bits are transmitted. Then, each $P_{i}$ in turn transmits a 1 if and only if the color it sees matches the color transmitted in the first $\log \left(\chi_{k}(n)\right)$ bits. Finally, the processes halt and accept if and only if every process braodcast a 1 in the last phase.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a colouring of S_n with no monochromatic forbidden pattern; P_0..P_{k-1} broadcast the colour of w_0, then each checks its own w_i's colour matches.

nodes.name: Fix colouring
nodes.statement: Color the hyperplane $S_{n}=\left\{\bar{v} \in H_{n} \mid \sum \bar{v}=n\right\}$ of $H_{n}$ with $\chi_{k}(n)$ colors such that no forbidden $k$-pattern is monochromatic.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a chi_k(n)-colouring of S_n avoiding monochromatic forbidden patterns.

nodes.name: Compute w_i
nodes.statement: Let $\left\langle v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right\rangle$ be a situation in $H_{n}$. Let process $P_{i}$ know every number but $v_{i}$. Each process $P_{i}$ computes the point $$ \bar{w}_{i}=\left\langle v_{0}, \ldots, v_{i-1}, n-\left(\sum_{j \neq i} v_{j}\right), v_{i+1}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right\rangle \in S_{n} . $$
nodes.statement_short: Each P_i completes its view to the point w_i of S_n.

nodes.name: Broadcast colour of w_0
nodes.statement: At time $t=0, P_{0}$ broadcasts bit 0 of the color at $\bar{w}_{0}$. At $t=1, P_{1}$ broadcasts bit 1 of the color at $\bar{w}_{1}$. This continues until $\log \left(\chi_{k}(n)\right)$ bits are transmitted.
nodes.statement_short: Transmit the log chi_k(n) bits of the colour of w_0, round robin.

nodes.name: Check colours
nodes.statement: Then, each $P_{i}$ in turn transmits a 1 if and only if the color it sees matches the color transmitted in the first $\log \left(\chi_{k}(n)\right)$ bits.
nodes.statement_short: Each P_i sends 1 iff its w_i has the broadcast colour.

nodes.name: Accept/reject
nodes.statement: Finally, the processes halt and accept if and only if every process braodcast a 1 in the last phase.
nodes.statement_short: Accept iff all sent 1.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.1 (validity of the coloring protocol)
nodes.statement: THEOREM 4.1. The above protocol is valid for Exactly-n.
conclusions: The above protocol is valid for Exactly-n

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: Proof. The points $\bar{w}_{i}$ are a forbidden $k$-pattern in $S_{n}$. Thus, if the processes agree that all are the same color, the points must coincide. Hence $\left\langle v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right\rangle \in S_{n}$ and the processes correctly accept. If $\left(v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right\rangle \notin S_{n}$, then the processes cannot all see the same color since the forbidden points are not monochromatic. Therefore, the processes correctly reject. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: The w_i form a forbidden pattern; same colours force them to coincide (accept on S_n), otherwise some colour differs (reject).

nodes.name: On S_n: accept
nodes.statement: The points $\bar{w}_{i}$ are a forbidden $k$-pattern in $S_{n}$. Thus, if the processes agree that all are the same color, the points must coincide. Hence $\left\langle v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right\rangle \in S_{n}$ and the processes correctly accept.
nodes.statement_short: If all colours agree, the w_i coincide, so v is on S_n and the processes accept.

nodes.name: Off S_n: reject
nodes.statement: If $\left(v_{0}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right\rangle \notin S_{n}$, then the processes cannot all see the same color since the forbidden points are not monochromatic. Therefore, the processes correctly reject. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Off S_n, the forbidden points are not monochromatic, so the processes reject.

nodes.name: Optimal protocol via exhaustive search
nodes.statement: Note that even though $\chi_{k}$ is not known, the optimal protocol can be implemented after an exhaustve search.

nodes.name: C_k(N)
nodes.statement: Definition. Let $C_{k}(N)$ be the minimum number of colors needed to color $1, \ldots, N$ such that no length- $k$ arithmetic progression is colored monochromatically.
nodes.statement_short: Minimum colours of {1..N} with no monochromatic k-term arithmetic progression.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.2 (chi_k(n) <= C_k(kn))
nodes.statement: Theorem 4.2. For $N=k n$, $$ \chi_{k}(n) \leq C_{k}(N) . $$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: Proof. Define the map $q$ from $S_{n}$ to $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ by $$ q\left(v_{0}, v_{1}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right)=v_{0}+2 v_{1}+\cdots+k \cdot v_{k-1} . $$ Color $1, \ldots, N$ with $c=C_{k}(N)$ colors, avoiding monochromatic length- $k$ arithmetic progressions. Color each $\bar{v} \in S_{n}$ with the color of $q(\bar{v})$. We prove by contradiction that this coloring of $S_{n}$ contains no monochromatic forbidden $k$-patterns. Assume $\bar{v}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}_{k-1}$ is a monochromatic forbidden $k$-pattern. By definition there is a $\bar{w} \in H_{n}$ such that $$ \bar{v}_{i}=\bar{w}+\lambda_{i} \bar{e}_{i}, $$ for some $\lambda_{0}, \ldots, \lambda_{k-1}$. Since each $\bar{v}_{i}$ is on $S_{n}$, it follows that $\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{1}=\cdots=\lambda_{k-1}$. Consider the points $$ q\left(\bar{v}_{0}\right), q\left(\bar{v}_{1}\right), \ldots, q\left(\bar{v}_{k-1}\right) . $$ The map $q$ is linear, so $q\left(\bar{v}_{i}\right)=q(\bar{w})+\lambda_{0} q\left(\bar{e}_{i}\right)$. By definition of $q$, $$ q\left(\bar{e}_{i}\right)=i+1 ; $$ hence $$ q\left(\bar{v}_{i}\right)=a+(i+1) b, $$ where $a=q(\bar{w})$ and $b=\lambda_{0}$. But then there is a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length $k$, which is a contradiction. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Pull back an AP-free colouring of {1..N} via the linear map q(v)=sum (i+1)v_i; a monochromatic forbidden pattern maps to a monochromatic k-term AP.

nodes.name: Define q
nodes.statement: Define the map $q$ from $S_{n}$ to $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ by $$ q\left(v_{0}, v_{1}, \ldots, v_{k-1}\right)=v_{0}+2 v_{1}+\cdots+k \cdot v_{k-1} . $$
nodes.statement_short: Define linear map q into {1..N}.

nodes.name: Pull back colouring
nodes.statement: Color $1, \ldots, N$ with $c=C_{k}(N)$ colors, avoiding monochromatic length- $k$ arithmetic progressions. Color each $\bar{v} \in S_{n}$ with the color of $q(\bar{v})$.
nodes.statement_short: Colour S_n by pulling back an AP-free colouring.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: We prove by contradiction that this coloring of $S_{n}$ contains no monochromatic forbidden $k$-patterns.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: no monochromatic forbidden pattern.

nodes.name: Assume pattern
nodes.statement: Assume $\bar{v}_{0}, \ldots, \bar{v}_{k-1}$ is a monochromatic forbidden $k$-pattern.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a monochromatic forbidden pattern.

nodes.name: Unfold definition
nodes.statement: By definition there is a $\bar{w} \in H_{n}$ such that $$ \bar{v}_{i}=\bar{w}+\lambda_{i} \bar{e}_{i}, $$ for some $\lambda_{0}, \ldots, \lambda_{k-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write v_i = w + lambda_i e_i.

nodes.name: Equal lambdas
nodes.statement: Since each $\bar{v}_{i}$ is on $S_{n}$, it follows that $\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{1}=\cdots=\lambda_{k-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lying on S_n forces all lambda_i equal.

nodes.name: Images form an AP
nodes.statement: Consider the points $$ q\left(\bar{v}_{0}\right), q\left(\bar{v}_{1}\right), \ldots, q\left(\bar{v}_{k-1}\right) . $$ The map $q$ is linear, so $q\left(\bar{v}_{i}\right)=q(\bar{w})+\lambda_{0} q\left(\bar{e}_{i}\right)$. By definition of $q$, $$ q\left(\bar{e}_{i}\right)=i+1 ; $$ hence $$ q\left(\bar{v}_{i}\right)=a+(i+1) b, $$ where $a=q(\bar{w})$ and $b=\lambda_{0}$.
nodes.statement_short: By linearity q(v_i)=a+(i+1)b, an arithmetic progression.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: But then there is a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length $k$, which is a contradiction. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Monochromatic k-AP contradicts the colouring.

nodes.name: Growth rate of C_k(N)
nodes.statement: Determining the true rate of growth of $C_{k}(N)$ is a difficult open problem.

nodes.name: Unboundedness of C_k (van der Waerden)
nodes.statement: It is known that $C_{k}$ is unbounded for fixed $k$, however, for $k \geq 4$ it can only be shown to grow extremely slowly.
conclusions: $C_{k}$ is unbounded
for $k \geq 4$ it can only be shown to grow extremely slowly

nodes.name: R_k(N)
nodes.statement: Definition. Let $R_{k}(N)$ be the size of a largest subset $A \subset\{1, \ldots, N\}$ that contains no length- $k$ arithmetic progression.
nodes.statement_short: Largest size of a k-AP-free subset of {1..N}.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.3 (C_k vs R_k)
nodes.statement: Theorem 4.3. For some constant $a>0$, $$ \frac{N}{R_{k}(N)} \leq C_{k}(N) \leq \frac{a N \lg N}{R_{k}(N)} \text {. } $$
conclusions: $$ \frac{N}{R_{k}(N)} \leq C_{k}(N) \leq \frac{a N \lg N}{R_{k}(N)} \text {. } $$
nodes.statement_short: C_k(N) is within a log N factor of N/R_k(N).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.3
nodes.statement: Proof. Suppose $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ can be $c$-colored in such a way that there are no length- $k$ arithmetic progressions. Then some color class must be used at least $N / c$ times. Therefore, $R_{k}(N) \geq N / c$. The first inequality holds since $c=C_{k}(N)$. Now, assume that $A$ is a subset of $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ that contains no arithmetic progressions of length $k$. We demonstrate that the second inequality holds by proving that it is possible to $c$-color $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ so that it has no length- $k$ arithmetic progressions provided $c \leq a N \lg N /|A|$. This follows directly from: Lemma 4.4. Let $A \subset\{1, \ldots, N\}$. No more than $O(N \lg N /|A|)$ translates of $A$ are needed to completely cover $\{1, \ldots, N\}$. Proof of Lemma: We use a probabilistic existence argument. Choose random translations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{\ell}$, with each $t_{i}$ in the interval $-N$ to $N$. The probability that a value $x \in\{1, \ldots, N\}$ is not covered by a particular translation is at most $1-|A| / 2 N$. Therefore, the expected number of missed values is bounded above by $$ N \cdot\left(1-\frac{|A|}{2 N}\right)^{\ell} . $$ For large enough $a$, choosing $\ell=a N \lg N /|A|$ makes this less than 1 and the Lemma is proved. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound by pigeonhole on colour classes; upper bound by covering {1..N} with few translates of an AP-free set (Lemma 4.4).

nodes.name: Pigeonhole
nodes.statement: Suppose $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ can be $c$-colored in such a way that there are no length- $k$ arithmetic progressions. Then some color class must be used at least $N / c$ times.
nodes.statement_short: Some colour class of an AP-free colouring has size >= N/c.

nodes.name: First inequality
nodes.statement: Therefore, $R_{k}(N) \geq N / c$. The first inequality holds since $c=C_{k}(N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence N/R_k(N) <= C_k(N).

nodes.name: Take AP-free A
nodes.statement: Now, assume that $A$ is a subset of $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ that contains no arithmetic progressions of length $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Take an AP-free set A.

nodes.name: Reduce to covering
nodes.statement: We demonstrate that the second inequality holds by proving that it is possible to $c$-color $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ so that it has no length- $k$ arithmetic progressions provided $c \leq a N \lg N /|A|$. This follows directly from:
nodes.statement_short: Second inequality reduces to covering by translates of A.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.4 and proof
nodes.statement: Lemma 4.4. Let $A \subset\{1, \ldots, N\}$. No more than $O(N \lg N /|A|)$ translates of $A$ are needed to completely cover $\{1, \ldots, N\}$. Proof of Lemma: We use a probabilistic existence argument. Choose random translations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{\ell}$, with each $t_{i}$ in the interval $-N$ to $N$. The probability that a value $x \in\{1, \ldots, N\}$ is not covered by a particular translation is at most $1-|A| / 2 N$. Therefore, the expected number of missed values is bounded above by $$ N \cdot\left(1-\frac{|A|}{2 N}\right)^{\ell} . $$ For large enough $a$, choosing $\ell=a N \lg N /|A|$ makes this less than 1 and the Lemma is proved. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Inner covering lemma and its proof.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.4 (covering by translates)
nodes.statement: Lemma 4.4. Let $A \subset\{1, \ldots, N\}$. No more than $O(N \lg N /|A|)$ translates of $A$ are needed to completely cover $\{1, \ldots, N\}$.
conclusions: No more than $O(N \lg N /|A|)$ translates of $A$ are needed to completely cover $\{1, \ldots, N\}$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement: Proof of Lemma: We use a probabilistic existence argument. Choose random translations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{\ell}$, with each $t_{i}$ in the interval $-N$ to $N$. The probability that a value $x \in\{1, \ldots, N\}$ is not covered by a particular translation is at most $1-|A| / 2 N$. Therefore, the expected number of missed values is bounded above by $$ N \cdot\left(1-\frac{|A|}{2 N}\right)^{\ell} . $$ For large enough $a$, choosing $\ell=a N \lg N /|A|$ makes this less than 1 and the Lemma is proved. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Random translates: expected number of uncovered points N(1-|A|/2N)^l < 1 for l = a N lg N/|A|.

nodes.name: Method
nodes.statement: We use a probabilistic existence argument.
nodes.statement_short: Probabilistic method.

nodes.name: Random translates
nodes.statement: Choose random translations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{\ell}$, with each $t_{i}$ in the interval $-N$ to $N$. The probability that a value $x \in\{1, \ldots, N\}$ is not covered by a particular translation is at most $1-|A| / 2 N$.
nodes.statement_short: Each translate misses a point with probability <= 1-|A|/2N.

nodes.name: Expected misses
nodes.statement: Therefore, the expected number of missed values is bounded above by $$ N \cdot\left(1-\frac{|A|}{2 N}\right)^{\ell} . $$
nodes.statement_short: Expected uncovered count N(1-|A|/2N)^l.

nodes.name: Choose l
nodes.statement: For large enough $a$, choosing $\ell=a N \lg N /|A|$ makes this less than 1 and the Lemma is proved. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Choose l so the expectation is below 1.

nodes.name: Roth's theorem (lower bound on R_3)
nodes.statement: THEOREM 4.5. (Roth $[R]) R_{3}(n)>n e^{-c \sqrt{\log n}}$.
conclusions: R_{3}(n)>n e^{-c \sqrt{\log n}}

nodes.name: Corollary 4.6 (three players need O(sqrt log n) bits)
nodes.statement: Corollary 4.6. Three players can determine Exactly$n$ in $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ bits.
conclusions: Three players can determine Exactly$n$ in $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ bits

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.6
nodes.statement: Proof. From the above, $$ \chi_{3}(n) \leq C_{3}(3 n) \leq a N \lg N / R_{3}(3 n) \leq a \lg n e^{c \sqrt{\log n}} . $$ Therefore, $\log \chi_{3}(n)$, the number of bits that have to be communicated, is $O(\sqrt{\log n})$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain Theorems 4.2, 4.3 and Roth's bound to get log chi_3(n) = O(sqrt(log n)).

nodes.name: Branching program
nodes.statement: DEFINITION. A branching program on the bits $b_{0}, \ldots, b_{n-1}$ is a rooted, directed, acyclic graph whose internal nodes are labeled with queries of the form "bit $b_{i}$ ?", whose edges are labeled with possible query answers " $b_{i}=0$ ", or " $b_{i}=1$ ", and whose leaves are labeled either "accept", or "reject".
differentia: whose internal nodes are labeled with queries of the form "bit $b_{i}$ ?"
whose edges are labeled with possible query answers " $b_{i}=0$ ", or " $b_{i}=1$ "
whose leaves are labeled either "accept", or "reject"

nodes.name: Acceptance by a branching program
nodes.statement: For a given assignment of zeroes and ones to the $b_{i}$, a branching program either accepts or rejects as the path defined by the bit values leads to an accept or reject leaf.

nodes.name: Time of a branching program
nodes.statement: Time for a branching program is the maximum path length from the root to a leaf.

nodes.name: Space of a branching program
nodes.statement: Space for a branching program is the maximum, over all $d$, of the number of vertices at distance $d$ from the root.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.1 (disjoint hidden blocks)
nodes.statement: Lemma 5.1. Let $P_{0}, \ldots, P_{k-1}$ be processes. Let $P_{i}$ have access to subset $s_{i}$ of the bits $\left\{b_{0}, \ldots, b_{n-1}\right\}$. If $\left|s_{i}\right| \leq \alpha \cdot n$, for some $\alpha<1$, i.e., if each process is missing at least a constant fraction of the bits, then there exists a constant $\beta$, and disjoint subsets $r_{0}, \ldots$, $r_{k-1}$ of the $b_{i}$ such that, \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $s_{i} \cap r_{i}=\emptyset$, i.e., process $P_{i}$ doesn't have access to bits in subset $r_{i}$, and \item[(ii)] $\left|r_{i}\right| \geq \beta \cdot n$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: Let $P_{i}$ have access to subset $s_{i}$ of the bits $\left\{b_{0}, \ldots, b_{n-1}\right\}$.
conclusions: there exists a constant $\beta$, and disjoint subsets $r_{0}, \ldots$, $r_{k-1}$ of the $b_{i}$ such that,
$s_{i} \cap r_{i}=\emptyset$
$\left|r_{i}\right| \geq \beta \cdot n$
nodes.statement_short: If each process misses a constant fraction of the bits, there are disjoint linear-size blocks r_i hidden from P_i.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: Proof. An iterated application of Hall's matching Theorem gives this result directly. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Iterate Hall's matching theorem.

nodes.name: Reduction to the integer-sharing model
nodes.statement: This means that if the bits outside the union of the $r_{i}$ are held constant, the $P_{i}$ share integers whose values are the number of bits "on" in the $r_{j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fixing bits outside the r_i, processes share integers counting ones in the r_j.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.2 (constant-space branching programs need super-linear length)
nodes.statement: Theorem 5.2. Any constant-space branching program requires super-linear length to compute Exactly-n.
conclusions: requires super-linear length to compute Exactly-n

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.2
nodes.statement: Proof. Suppose not. Then, for some integers $c, d$ there are branching programs of width $d$ and length $c \cdot n$ that accept Exactly- $n$. Think of a branching program of length $c \cdot n$ as being composed of $2 c d$ equally-long segments. Each segment can be thought of as a process, $P_{i}$, that has access to no more than $n / 2$ bits. The whole branching program can thus be viewed as $2 c d$ processes, each missing $1 / 2$ the bits, communicating a constant amount of information $(2 c d \log d$ bits) and determining Exactly- $n$. Using Lemma 5.1 we can show that this contradicts Theorem 3.3.
nodes.statement_short: Cut a width-d, length-cn program into 2cd segments viewed as processes each missing half the bits; Lemma 5.1 then contradicts Theorem 3.3.

nodes.name: Assume linear length
nodes.statement: Suppose not. Then, for some integers $c, d$ there are branching programs of width $d$ and length $c \cdot n$ that accept Exactly- $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume width-d, length-cn programs for Exactly-n.

nodes.name: Segments as processes
nodes.statement: Think of a branching program of length $c \cdot n$ as being composed of $2 c d$ equally-long segments. Each segment can be thought of as a process, $P_{i}$, that has access to no more than $n / 2$ bits.
nodes.statement_short: Split into 2cd segments, each a process seeing at most n/2 bits.

nodes.name: Constant communication
nodes.statement: The whole branching program can thus be viewed as $2 c d$ processes, each missing $1 / 2$ the bits, communicating a constant amount of information $(2 c d \log d$ bits) and determining Exactly- $n$.
nodes.statement_short: The program becomes an MPP with 2cd log d bits.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Using Lemma 5.1 we can show that this contradicts Theorem 3.3.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.1 and Theorem 3.3 give a contradiction.

nodes.name: Corollary 5.3 (Threshold needs super-linear time)
nodes.statement: Corollary 5.3. Any constant-space branching program for Threshold requires greater than linear time.
assumptions: Any constant-space branching program for Threshold
conclusions: requires greater than linear time
